profile.summary: The Jores plant promoter CNN is a pair of convolutional neural networks that predict how strongly a plant core promoter drives gene expression. Each model takes a 170-base promoter sequence (from 165 bases upstream to 5 bases downstream of the transcription start site) and outputs a single number, the promoter strength measured by STARR-seq. One model was trained on measurements in tobacco leaves and the other on maize protoplasts, using promoters from Arabidopsis, maize and sorghum.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Results, Computational modelling of promoter strength; Methods, Library design and construction; notebook: Build the models; README: folders

summary_quotes.text: To build a direct sequence to promoter strength model we built a CNN using the tensorflow (v.2.2) package in python.
These 170-bp regions were tested for promoter strength by using them to drive expression of a barcoded green fluorescent protein (GFP) reporter gene
For this study, we used the sequence from −165 to +5 relative to the annotated TSS as core promoters.
To predict promoter strength, we built separate models for the tobacco leaf and the maize protoplast system.

The folder 'promoter_annotation' contains the code to extract promoter sequences from the Arabidopsis, maize and sorghum genomes.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The sequence is one-hot encoded and passed to two forward- and reverse-strand scan layers, adapted from DeepGMAP, with 128 filters of width 13. These feed a standard convolutional layer (128 filters, width 13, ReLU). Each convolutional layer is followed by dropout at rate 0.15. A dense layer of 64 units with batch normalisation and ReLU leads to a final dense layer with one output. The first convolutional kernel is initialised with clustered transcription factor and core promoter element motifs. The models are trained as regressions with mean squared error loss on the measured enrichment, with Adam, early stopping and learning-rate reduction.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Computational modelling of promoter strength; notebook: Build the models

quotes.text: The model consists of two forward- and reverse-sequence scan layers adapted from DeepGMAP

with 128 filters and a kernel width of 13 that feed into a regular convolutional layer (128 filters, kernel width 13, ReLU activation). Each convolutional layer is followed by a dropout layer with a 0.15 dropout rate.

The output of the convolutional layers is fed into a dense layer with 64 filters with batch-normalization and ReLU activation that is followed by a final dense layer generating the single output. We initialized the first convolutional layer kernel with the clustered TF motifs.

sections.title: Use for promoter design
sections.body: The authors used the models for in silico evolution. In each round, every single-nucleotide variant of a promoter is scored and the best is kept for the next round. Scoring can use the tobacco model, the maize model, or the mean of both. The authors synthesised and tested promoters after three and ten rounds. They report a large rise in measured strength after three rounds and a smaller further rise after ten, and that the averaged score gave promoters active in both systems.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, Computational modelling of promoter strength; Methods, In silico evolution of promoter sequences

quotes.text: In each round, we generated all possible single nucleotide variants of a given promoter, scored them with the CNN models and kept the variant with the highest predicted activity for the next round.
with both models in which case the mean of both predictions was used to select the best-performing variant
As predicted, we observed a large increase in promoter strength after three rounds of evolution and another, albeit less pronounced, increase after ten rounds
Moreover, a combination of CNN models trained on data from the tobacco and maize assay systems yielded promoters active in both systems.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two trained models are committed to the repository as TensorFlow SavedModel folders: CNN/model_leaf (tobacco leaf) and CNN/model_proto (maize protoplast). The training and test tables used are in the same folder. The notebook loads a saved model if its folder exists and trains a new one otherwise. A result should name the model (leaf or proto) and the repository commit; this page read commit ace4ead5.
